Expectation1: Follow safety and hygiene protocols at all times.
Situation1: They wear gloves occasionally when handling certain cleaning tasks.
Expectation2: Raise public awareness about social inequities and marginalized groups
Situation2: They respond to an urgent incident of discrimination that requires immediate public attention and awareness.
Story: I was halfway through scrubbing the hospital corridor, the faint scent of bleach clinging to my gloves, when my phone buzzed in my pocket. I hesitated, glancing at the clock—my break was still twenty minutes away, and I was supposed to be wearing gloves at all times, especially with the new hygiene protocols. But the message was urgent: a friend from the advocacy group had witnessed a blatant act of discrimination in the waiting room, and they needed someone to speak up, to post, to rally support right now. My heart pounded. As a cleaner, I was expected to keep my hands gloved, my focus on safety, my presence almost invisible. As an advocate, I was supposed to be visible, loud, and immediate, especially for those who had no voice. I stared at my gloved hands, torn between the rules of my job and the call to action that defined my other life. The mop handle felt heavy, my phone heavier still, as I stood in the corridor, wrestling with the impossible expectations pressing in from both sides.
